blocks.text: A tall young man collapses with sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. His erect chest film looks nearly normal at first glance, until you notice a thin white line near the right apex with no lung markings beyond it. Spotting that line depends on a habit: look at every film in the same order, every time.

blocks.markdown: The chest radiograph is the most requested film in medicine. A **posteroanterior (PA)** film is taken with the X-ray beam entering the back and exiting the front onto the detector, with the patient standing and the heart close to the detector. This limits magnification of the heart. Anteroposterior (AP) films, common on wards, magnify the heart and mediastinum.

blocks.title: Systematic review
blocks.text: A fixed order of inspection that makes sure no area is skipped. A common mnemonic is ABCDE: Airway (trachea, bronchi), Breathing (lungs and pleura), Circulation (heart, mediastinum and hila), Diaphragm (including costophrenic angles and any free air), and Everything else (bones, soft tissues, lines and tubes).

blocks.markdown: Before interpreting, check the **technical quality**. Is the patient correctly identified? Is the film **rotated**? The medial ends of the clavicles should be equidistant from the spinous processes. Is the inspiration adequate? About six anterior ribs or ten posterior ribs should be visible above the diaphragm. Is the exposure adequate? The vertebral bodies should be just visible behind the heart. A poor-quality film can mimic or hide disease.

items: Airway: is the trachea central and are the main bronchi patent?
Breathing: compare the lung zones, look for opacities, and trace the pleural edge.
Circulation: assess heart size, the borders, the aortic knuckle and the hila.
Diaphragm: smooth domes, sharp costophrenic angles, no air beneath.
Everything else: ribs, clavicles, spine, soft tissues, lines.

blocks.markdown: **Cardiac borders.** On a PA film the right heart border is formed by the right atrium (with the superior vena cava forming the right upper mediastinal edge). The left border from top to bottom is the aortic knuckle (aortic arch), the pulmonary trunk, the left atrial appendage and the left ventricle. The **cardiothoracic ratio** is the maximal cardiac width divided by the maximal internal thoracic width, and on a PA film is normally less than 0.5.

blocks.caption: Cardiothoracic ratio; above 0.5 suggests cardiomegaly on a PA film.

blocks.title: Calculating the cardiothoracic ratio
blocks.prompt: On a PA film the widest part of the heart measures 13.5 cm and the widest internal thoracic diameter is 30.0 cm. Is the heart enlarged?

steps.text: Identify the cardiac width, 13.5 cm, and the thoracic width, 30.0 cm.
Divide the cardiac width by the thoracic width.
Compare with the PA threshold of 0.5: 0.45 is less than 0.5, so the heart is not enlarged.

blocks.answer: CTR 0.45, normal on a PA film.

blocks.markdown: **Hila and costophrenic angles.** The hila are formed mainly by the pulmonary arteries and veins, with the main bronchi in the centre. The left hilum is normally slightly higher than the right. They should be of similar density and size. The **costophrenic angles** are the sharp angles where the diaphragm meets the chest wall laterally; they are normally acute and clear.

rows: Thin visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it
Dense opacity with a meniscus rising up the lateral chest wall
Large tension pneumothorax pushes it away
Large effusion pushes it away from the fluid
blocks.caption: Radiographic features of a pneumothorax and a pleural effusion on an erect film.

blocks.title: Reading a lung-edge line
blocks.prompt: An erect film shows a thin white line parallel to the chest wall in the left apical region; beyond it there are no lung markings and the lung appears smaller. The trachea is central. What is the finding and how would you recognise tension?

steps.text: The line is the visceral pleural edge and the area beyond is air with no vessels: a pneumothorax.
Air rises on an erect film, so the apex is the most sensitive place to look.
Signs of tension are mediastinal and tracheal shift away from the side, flattening of the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm and a widened rib space.
Here the trachea is central, so there is no evidence of tension on this film, although tension is a clinical diagnosis.

blocks.answer: Left pneumothorax without radiographic signs of tension.

blocks.title: Fluid and air behave differently
blocks.text: Air rises and collapses the lung away from the chest wall; fluid sinks and blunts the costophrenic angle with a meniscus. Both can displace the mediastinum if large.

blocks.title: Supine films hide effusions
blocks.text: On a supine film pleural fluid layers posteriorly and may appear only as a hazy increased density over a hemithorax, and a pneumothorax collects anteriorly, so these signs can be missed.

points: Use a fixed systematic approach and check rotation, inspiration and penetration first.
The right heart border is right atrium; the left border runs aortic knuckle, pulmonary trunk, left atrial appendage and left ventricle; CTR is normally below 0.5 on a PA film.
Pneumothorax shows a visceral pleural line with absent markings beyond; effusion shows blunted costophrenic angle and a meniscus.

questions.stem: Which structure forms the right heart border on a normal PA chest radiograph?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the right atrium forms the right heart border.
distractorRationale.b: The right ventricle lies anteriorly and forms the lower anterior surface, not the right border.
distractorRationale.c: The left atrial appendage lies on the left border.
distractorRationale.d: The aortic knuckle forms part of the left upper mediastinal contour.

questions.explanation: On a PA film the right atrium forms the right heart border, with the SVC above it. The right ventricle is seen on the lateral view anteriorly.

questions.stem: In order from superior to inferior, which structures form the left mediastinal border on a PA film?

options.text: Aortic knuckle, pulmonary trunk, left atrial appendage, left ventricle
Left ventricle, left atrial appendage, pulmonary trunk, aortic knuckle
Pulmonary trunk, aortic knuckle, left ventricle, left atrial appendage
Aortic knuckle, left ventricle, pulmonary trunk, left atrial appendage

questions.correctOptionText: Aortic knuckle, pulmonary trunk, left atrial appendage, left ventricle

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the order from top is aortic knuckle, pulmonary trunk, left atrial appendage, left ventricle.
distractorRationale.c: The pulmonary trunk lies below the aortic knuckle.
distractorRationale.d: The left ventricle is at the bottom, not between knuckle and trunk.

questions.explanation: The left heart border runs from the aortic arch down through the pulmonary trunk and left atrial appendage to the left ventricle. Learning this sequence helps localise an abnormal bulge.

questions.stem: On a PA chest film the maximal cardiac width is 16.2 cm and the maximal internal thoracic width is 30.0 cm. Calculate the cardiothoracic ratio (a dimensionless number).
questions.explanation: CTR = 16.2 divided by 30.0 = 0.54. This exceeds 0.5, so it suggests cardiomegaly on a PA film, although an AP film would magnify the heart and make the threshold unreliable.

questions.stem: A film shows the medial ends of the clavicles lying at unequal distances from the spinous processes of the vertebrae. What technical problem does this indicate?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: unequal clavicle distances indicate rotation.
distractorRationale.b: Inspiration is judged by rib count.
distractorRationale.c: Penetration is judged by visibility of the vertebrae through the heart.
distractorRationale.d: As above, not related to clavicle distance.

questions.explanation: Rotation shifts the mediastinum and can alter the apparent size or shape of structures. The clavicle heads should be equidistant from the spinous processes.

questions.stem: An erect film of a patient with chest pain shows a meniscus-shaped opacity at the left base, with blunting of the left costophrenic angle, and the trachea displaced to the right. Which is the best interpretation?

options.text: Left lower lobe collapse with shift toward the lesion

distractorRationale.a: Correct: blunted angle and meniscus indicate an effusion; the large volume pushes the mediastinum away.
distractorRationale.b: A pneumothorax shows absent markings and a pleural line, not a meniscus.
distractorRationale.c: Blunting and a meniscus are not normal.
distractorRationale.d: Collapse pulls the trachea toward the lesion, not away.

questions.explanation: A meniscus and blunted costophrenic angle indicate pleural fluid. A large effusion pushes the mediastinum and trachea to the opposite side, whereas collapse pulls them toward the diseased side.

questions.stem: Which finding on an erect chest film indicates a pneumothorax?

options.text: A thin visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it
A meniscus at the lung base

questions.correctOptionText: A thin visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a visible pleural edge with absent markings is characteristic.
distractorRationale.c: An enlarged heart outline points to cardiomegaly or a pericardial effusion, not air in the pleural space.

questions.explanation: Air in the pleural space separates the lung from the chest wall. The collapsed lung edge appears as a thin line with no vessels peripheral to it.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man has a large right pneumothorax. Which additional film finding would suggest that it is under tension?

options.text: Trachea and mediastinum shifted to the left, with a flattened right hemidiaphragm
Trachea shifted to the right toward the pneumothorax
Blunted right costophrenic angle with a meniscus
Sharp costophrenic angles bilaterally with the trachea central

questions.correctOptionText: Trachea and mediastinum shifted to the left, with a flattened right hemidiaphragm

distractorRationale.a: Correct: tension pushes the mediastinum away from the affected side and flattens the ipsilateral diaphragm.
distractorRationale.b: A shift toward the affected side suggests volume loss, not tension.
distractorRationale.c: A meniscus and blunted angle indicate fluid.
distractorRationale.d: Central trachea and sharp angles indicate no shift.

questions.explanation: In tension the trapped air pushes the mediastinum away from the pneumothorax and depresses or flattens the hemidiaphragm. Tension is a clinical emergency, so these signs should be recognised promptly.

questions.stem: On a normal PA chest radiograph, the left hilum lies slightly higher than the right.
questions.explanation: The left pulmonary artery arches over the left main bronchus, placing the left hilum slightly higher than the right. A reversal of this arrangement suggests volume loss or a mass.

questions.stem: Outline the systematic approach you would use to review a chest radiograph and explain why technical quality is assessed first.
markingGuide: Check identity, rotation, inspiration and penetration.
Diaphragm and costophrenic angles, then everything else (bones, soft tissues, lines).
Poor technique can mimic disease or hide it.
questions.explanation: A fixed order prevents omissions and satisfaction of search. Technical faults such as rotation or poor inspiration alter apparent anatomy, so they must be recognised first.

questions.stem: A supine ward film is requested after a road traffic accident. Explain how a pleural effusion and a pneumothorax may appear differently on a supine film than on an erect film.
markingGuide: Fluid layers posteriorly on a supine film, giving hazy increased density over the hemithorax.
Blunting of the costophrenic angle may be absent.
Air collects anteriorly and may not reach the apex.
A deep costophrenic sulcus can be a clue to pneumothorax.
Erect films show fluid at the base with a meniscus and air at the apex.
questions.explanation: The patient's position decides where fluid and air collect. When supine, both are spread across the thorax and may not form the classical edge or meniscus, making them easy to miss.
